Name: David Tussey
Question: If a US naval aviator who was already a fully qualified attorney. If through injury acquired night blindness at rank of lieutenant commander and unable to fly. Is it possible for him to transfer to JAG corps?
Answer: In all likelihood, the USN would want to reassign that person to a non-flying but aviation related position, such as a Maintenance Officer, air intelligence, personnel administration, aviation supply, something along those lines. Those kinds of positions are directly combat related and there is always a need for them. The JAG corp is typically pretty full with fully qualified applicants, and there’s not a great need for additional, marginally experienced personnel. So I would say it’s possible, but unlikely. It’s not an area in the Navy that has a critical need — unlike the other positions I’ve enumerated. If you’re an LCDR Naval Aviator, you’ve got a ton of time, $s, and experience invested in you, and the US Navy is likely to want to recoup that in what they would consider a more meaningful, combat-related, aviation-related positions. Any officer that that level and experience would have a lot…a lot…to offer. BTW…such an officer would certainly be allowed to continue to wear his wings. They earned them.

Name: David Tussey
Question: Can US Navy fighter jets and other naval aviation provide close air support on the ground like US Marine Corps fighter jets, and naval aviation?
Answer: For sure. In fact CAS is a primary mission for both USN and USMC fighter squadrons. However, CAS today is much different than what you might see in a WWII film or even in the Iraq wars of the 1990s. Today, the threat to aircraft from ground forces is such that CAS missions demand stand-off and use of precision guided weapons. USN and USMC squadrons frequently train and operate together. USN and USMC pilots wear the same gold wings and receive the same training (as do USCG pilots also). USMC fighter squadrons even routinely deploy onboard aircraft carriers. And they certainly deploy onboard USN amphibious ships.

Name: David Tussey
Question: Why does the United States continue to use F-16 fighters instead of newer models like the F-22 and F-35?
Answer: The F-35 is replacing the F-16. It’s going a bit more slowly than originally planned for a number of reasons. Lockheed-Martin is continuing to increase the yearly production. Currently there is a backlog of over 200 aircraft. Keep in mind that the F-35 is being fielded by the USAF, USN, USMC and a large group of allied countries. It has proven to be a remarkable aircraft. And it is receiving ongoing upgrades. The F-22 is not currently in production and has not been in production since 2011. Less than 200 were produced.

Name: David Tussey
Question: Which aircraft is being considered as a replacement for the U.S. Navy's aging fleet of EA/F-18 Super Hornets, the Lockheed Martin F/A-XX or Boeing's Advanced Super Hornet?
Answer: Well the Navy is trying to replace the Super Hornet with the F-35, or at least have 1–2 squadrons of F-35s in every airwing. But the Super Hornet will be around for awhile, as there are orders for new Block III models in the works for the next couple of years. So those aircraft are not “aging”, in fact they’re brand new. The NGAD (Navalized) aircraft is still likely years away, and no idea how much it will cost or how fast it can be produced…or even how many will be needed. In the meantime, the F-35 is the Navy’s replacement, although it’s slow going.
